questions.question: What does the writing rule "Show, don't tell" mean?
options: Reveal feelings through actions and details instead of stating them directly
Always include pictures in your story
Tell the reader exactly what every character feels
Show your text to a friend before handing it in
questions.explanation: Instead of telling ("John was angry"), you show it through actions and body language ("John slammed his fist on the table, his face turning red").

questions.question: Which sentence is an example of "showing" rather than "telling"?
options: Her hands trembled as she pressed her back against the cold wall.
She was scared.
She felt fear.
She was very, very frightened.
questions.explanation: Showing uses actions, body language and sensory details to let the reader experience the feeling, instead of naming it directly.

questions.question: What is the climax in a story's plot structure?
options: The turning point - the most intense moment of the story
The introduction of characters and setting
The part where the conflict is resolved
The first sentence of the story
questions.explanation: The plot curve goes: exposition, rising action, climax (the turning point), falling action and resolution.

questions.question: What happens in the exposition of a narrative?
options: Characters, time and place are introduced
The conflict reaches its peak
The conflict is resolved
The story ends with a cliffhanger
questions.explanation: The exposition (introduction) presents the characters, the setting and the situation before the action builds up.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a good story opening?
options: To grab the reader's attention and make them want to read on
To summarise the whole plot immediately
To list all the characters' names
To explain the moral of the story
questions.explanation: A good opening hooks the reader - for example with action, dialogue or an intriguing question - so they want to continue reading.
